records.explanation: All sixteen classifications follow from parity, injectivity, periodicity, and continuity tests; the complete justification is given in the worked solution.
records.workedSolution:
For oddness,
\[
f_1(-x)=-f_1(x),\qquad f_2(-x)=(-x)\cos(-x)=-x\cos x=-f_2(x),
\]
whereas \(f_3(x)=3e^{2x}\) is not odd and
\[
f_4(x)=x-|x|=\begin{cases}2x,&x<0,\\0,&x\ge0,\end{cases}
\]
is not odd. Thus (a) is **Yes, Yes, No, No**.

For inverses, \(f_1\) and the strictly increasing \(f_3\) are one-to-one. The function \(f_2\) is not one-to-one because \(f_2(\pi/2)=f_2(3\pi/2)=0\), and \(f_4\) is constant on \([0,\infty)\). Thus (b) is **Yes, No, Yes, No**.

No function is periodic: \(f_1,f_3,f_4\) plainly have no positive period, and the factor \(x\) prevents \(x\cos x\) from being periodic. Thus (c) is **No, No, No, No**.

The first three functions are continuous at \(0\). For \(f_4\),
\[
\lim_{x\to0^-}2x=0=\lim_{x\to0^+}0=f_4(0).
\]
Thus (d) is **Yes, Yes, Yes, Yes**.
records.alternativeSolution:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
 & f_1&f_2&f_3&f_4\\\hline
\text{odd}&Y&Y&N&N\\
\text{invertible}&Y&N&Y&N\\
\text{periodic}&N&N&N&N\\
\text{continuous at }0&Y&Y&Y&Y
\end{array}
\]
This table follows directly from the parity identities, the two repeated-value counterexamples, and the piecewise form of \(f_4\).

records.explanation: Differentiate the position, factor the velocity and acceleration, and use sign changes to distinguish a stop from a direction reversal.
records.workedSolution:
\[
v(t)=x'(t)=12t^3-48t^2+48t=12t(t-2)^2,
\]
\[
a(t)=v'(t)=36t^2-96t+48=12(3t-2)(t-2).
\]
Hence the particle is at rest at \(t=0,2\). Since \((t-2)^2\ge0\), the sign of \(v\) is the sign of \(t\): \(v<0\) on \([-5,0)\) and \(v>0\) on \((0,2)\cup(2,5]\). Therefore direction changes only at \(t=0\); the double zero at \(t=2\) causes no reversal.

Acceleration first vanishes at \(t=2/3\) (the other zero is \(2\)), and
\[
v\!\left(\frac23\right)
=12\left(\frac23\right)\left(-\frac43\right)^2
=\frac{128}{9}.
\]
records.alternativeSolution: A sign chart for \(v(t)=12t(t-2)^2\) gives the direction immediately: the squared factor never changes sign, so only crossing \(t=0\) reverses the motion. Then factor \(a(t)=12(3t-2)(t-2)\), select the first zero \(2/3\), and substitute into the factored velocity.

records.prompt:
Let
\[
f(x)=\frac{1}{x}+\ln x,
\]
defined for
\[
e^{-1}\le x<e.
\]

partsPatches.label: (a)
partsPatches.answer: Since \(f'(x)=\dfrac{x-1}{x^2}\), the function decreases on \([e^{-1},1]\) and increases on \([1,e)\). The absolute maximum is \(f(e^{-1})=e-1\), and the absolute minimum is \(f(1)=1\). The point \(x=e\) is excluded; \(\lim_{x\to e^-}f(x)=1+e^{-1}\) is not attained.

partsPatches.label: (b)
partsPatches.answer: \(f''(x)=\dfrac{2-x}{x^3}\). The graph is concave up on \((e^{-1},2)\), concave down on \((2,e)\), and has an inflection point at \(\left(2,\tfrac12+\ln2\right)\).

partsPatches.label: (c)
partsPatches.prompt: Sketch the graph of \(f\) on \([e^{-1},e)\), showing the absolute extrema, the change in concavity, and the open endpoint at \(x=e\).
partsPatches.answer: The curve decreases from the closed point \((e^{-1},e-1)\) to the absolute minimum \((1,1)\), then increases toward the excluded endpoint \((e,1+e^{-1})\), which is drawn open. It is concave up until \(x=2\), has an inflection point at \(\left(2,\tfrac12+\ln2\right)\), and is concave down thereafter.

partsPatches.label: (d)
partsPatches.prompt: The average value of \(f\) on the interval is \(\dfrac{2}{e-1}\). State a geometrical interpretation of this number relative to the graph.
partsPatches.answer: The horizontal line \(y=\dfrac{2}{e-1}\) is the height of a rectangle with base from \(x=e^{-1}\) to \(x=e\) whose area equals the area under the graph of \(f\). Excluding the single endpoint \(x=e\) does not change the definite integral or the average value.

records.explanation: The source uses a half-open domain. Derivative and endpoint analysis gives the extrema and shape, and direct integration gives the stated average value.
records.workedSolution:
On the source domain \(e^{-1}\le x<e\),
\[
f'(x)=\frac{x-1}{x^2},\qquad f''(x)=\frac{2-x}{x^3}.
\]
Thus \(f\) decreases on \([e^{-1},1]\) and increases on \([1,e)\). Therefore
\[
f(e^{-1})=e-1\quad\text{(absolute maximum)},\qquad f(1)=1\quad\text{(absolute minimum)}.
\]
The excluded point \(x=e\) is not an endpoint candidate; \(\lim_{x\to e^-}f(x)=1+e^{-1}\).

Because \(x>0\), the graph is concave up on \((e^{-1},2)\), concave down on \((2,e)\), and has inflection point
\[
\left(2,\frac12+\ln2\right).
\]
The sketch begins at the closed point \((e^{-1},e-1)\), passes through the minimum \((1,1)\), changes concavity at \(x=2\), and approaches the open point \((e,1+e^{-1})\).

Finally,
\[
\int\left(\frac1x+\ln x\right)dx=\ln x+x\ln x-x,
\]
so
\[
\int_{e^{-1}}^e f(x)\,dx=2+\frac2e,\qquad e-e^{-1}=\frac{e^2-1}{e},
\]
and the average value is
\[
\frac{2+2/e}{e-e^{-1}}=\frac2{e-1}.
\]
It is the height of an equal-area rectangle over the base from \(e^{-1}\) to \(e\); omitting the single endpoint \(e\) does not change the integral.
records.alternativeSolution:
The sign charts \(f':-\,,0,\,+\) at \(x=1\) and \(f'':+\,,0,\,-\) at \(x=2\) determine the entire sketch. As a check on the average value,
\[
\frac2{e-1}\left(e-e^{-1}\right)=2+\frac2e,
\]
which equals the definite integral.

records.explanation: Differentiate the population model to locate the population maximum, then differentiate the rate to locate its minimum.
records.workedSolution:
\[
N'(t)=50(20-t)e^{-t/20}.
\]
Hence \(N\) increases to \(t=20\) and then decreases. Comparing the critical value and endpoints,
\[
N(20)=25000+\frac{20000}{e},\quad N(0)=25000,\quad
N(100)=1000(25+100e^{-5})>25000.
\]
Thus the greatest population is \(25000+20000/e\) at \(t=20\), and the least is \(25000\) at \(t=0\).

For the rate \(R=N'\),
\[
R'(t)=N''(t)=\frac52(t-40)e^{-t/20}.
\]
Therefore \(R\) decreases until \(t=40\) and increases afterward, so
\[
\min R=R(40)=50(-20)e^{-2}=-\frac{1000}{e^2}.
\]
records.alternativeSolution: Let \(u=t/20\). Then \(N=25000+20000ue^{-u}\), whose variable factor has derivative \(e^{-u}(1-u)\), giving \(t=20\). Also \(N'=1000(1-u)e^{-u}\); differentiating with respect to \(u\) gives a factor \(u-2\), hence the minimum rate occurs at \(t=40\).

records.explanation: Find the intersections, integrate top minus bottom for area, and use washers or shells for the volume about the y-axis.
records.workedSolution:
The curves meet at \(x=0,2\), and \(2x\ge x^2\) there. Hence
\[
A=\int_0^2(2x-x^2)\,dx
=\left[x^2-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2
=\frac43.
\]
For rotation about the \(y\)-axis, \(0\le y\le4\), with outer radius \(\sqrt y\) and inner radius \(y/2\). Thus
\[
V=\pi\int_0^4\left(y-\frac{y^2}{4}\right)dy
=\frac{8\pi}{3}.
\]
records.alternativeSolution:
Using shells,
\[
V=2\pi\int_0^2x(2x-x^2)\,dx
=2\pi\left[\frac{2x^3}{3}-\frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^2
=\frac{8\pi}{3},
\]
confirming the washer result.

records.explanation: Determine the symmetric parabolic and cosine models from the width and height, integrate each, and compare the exact areas.
records.workedSolution:
With endpoints \((\pm b,0)\) and vertex \((0,h)\), the parabolic arch is
\[
y=h\left(1-\frac{x^2}{b^2}\right).
\]
The cosine arch with the same endpoints and height is
\[
y=h\cos\left(\frac{\pi x}{2b}\right).
\]
Their areas are
\[
A_P=\int_{-b}^{b}h\left(1-\frac{x^2}{b^2}\right)dx=\frac{4bh}{3},
\]
\[
A_C=\int_{-b}^{b}h\cos\left(\frac{\pi x}{2b}\right)dx=\frac{4bh}{\pi}.
\]
Since \(\pi>3\), \(A_P>A_C\); the parabolic window has the greater area.
records.alternativeSolution:
Put \(x=bu\). Then
\[
A_P=bh\int_{-1}^{1}(1-u^2)\,du=\frac{4bh}{3},\qquad
A_C=bh\int_{-1}^{1}\cos\left(\frac{\pi u}{2}\right)du=\frac{4bh}{\pi}.
\]
The comparison is independent of the actual dimensions.

records.explanation: Differentiate the exponential curve, form the tangent at x equals r, solve for its x-intercept, and take the absolute horizontal distance.
records.workedSolution:
Let
\[
f(x)=\frac12(e^x+e^{-x}),\qquad f'(x)=\frac12(e^x-e^{-x}).
\]
The graph is even, has minimum \((0,1)\), and is concave up everywhere because \(f''=f>0\).

At \(R=(r,f(r))\), the tangent is
\[
y-f(r)=f'(r)(x-r).
\]
Setting \(y=0\) gives
\[
x_Q=r-\frac{f(r)}{f'(r)}
=r-\frac{e^r+e^{-r}}{e^r-e^{-r}}
=r-\coth r,
\]
so \(Q=(r-\coth r,0)\). With \(P=(r,0)\),
\[
PQ=|x_Q-r|=|\coth r|.
\]
As \(r\to\infty\),
\[
PQ=\frac{1+e^{-2r}}{1-e^{-2r}}\longrightarrow1.
\]
records.alternativeSolution:
Without hyperbolic notation,
\[
PQ=\left|\frac{e^{2r}+1}{e^{2r}-1}\right|.
\]
For \(r\to\infty\), divide by \(e^{2r}\) to obtain \((1+e^{-2r})/(1-e^{-2r})\to1\). The absolute value is essential when \(r<0\).
